Registering a server-side method and running against a live federation

method-registration-live-federation.Rmd

This walkthrough shows the full life cycle of a server-side DataSHIELD method: what it is, how an operator registers it on the nodes, and how a researcher then uses it — here against the live public federation at *.datashield.live (three sites: Nairobi, Dakar, Douala, holding the Breast-Cancer-Wisconsin demo table).

Every output block below was captured from a real run against that federation (dsFlower 0.2.4). None of it is executed at build time — reproduce it yourself with your own credentials.

1. The DataSHIELD trust model in one paragraph

A DataSHIELD analyst can only invoke functions that the node’s Opal server has explicitly whitelisted — the parser rejects anything else. So adding new server-side capability is two steps: (1) install the R package on the node’s compute container, and (2) register its methods with Opal so clients are allowed to call them. The raw data never leaves the node; only the method’s disclosure-controlled aggregate does.

We use one concrete method as the example: flowerFeatureStatsDS from dsFlower.

2. The example method: flowerFeatureStatsDS

dsFlower enforces differential privacy on federated model training. DP-SGD clips each per-sample gradient to a fixed norm, so on raw features the large-scale columns dominate and the model collapses — the cure is feature standardization. To standardize soundly across sites, the client needs the global per-feature mean/SD. That is what flowerFeatureStatsDS provides: a disclosure-controlled aggregate returning per-feature count / sum / sumsq (exactly what ds.mean/ds.var release), gated on the node’s minimum-rows threshold. It is a separate sanctioned aggregate — it is not part of, and does not weaken, the DP-SGD (epsilon, delta) budget.

flowerFeatureStatsDS <- function(data_symbol, feature_columns = NULL) {
  obj <- get(data_symbol, envir = parent.frame(), inherits = FALSE)
  .assertMinSamples(nrow(obj), min_n = .disclosure_min_rows())   # disclosure gate
  feats <- .ds_arg(feature_columns)
  # ... per-feature finite count / sum / sum-of-squares (per-feature gated) ...
  list(features = feats, n = n, sum = s, sumsq = ss)
}

For Opal to accept the call, the function is declared in the package’s DESCRIPTION under AggregateMethods: and exported in NAMESPACE.

3. Registering the method (operator, with admin rights)

First install the package on each node’s rock/compute container:

# On the node (shell): install into the rock's R library
# R CMD INSTALL --library=/var/lib/rock/R/library dsFlower_0.2.4.tar.gz

Then register its methods with Opal using opalr (admin credentials). One call publishes all of the package’s aggregate/assign methods from its DESCRIPTION:

library(opalr)
opts  <- list(ssl_verifyhost = 0L, ssl_verifypeer = 0L)
hosts <- c("nairobi", "dakar", "douala")

for (h in hosts) {
  o <- opal.login("administrator", Sys.getenv("OPAL_ADMIN_PW"),
                  url = paste0("https://", h, ".datashield.live"), opts = opts)
  dsadmin.set_package_methods(o, "dsFlower")          # registers every dsFlower method
  opal.logout(o)
}

To register (or inspect) a single method instead, use dsadmin.set_method() / dsadmin.get_methods(). Here is the method showing up in Opal’s aggregate table after registration:

o <- opal.login("administrator", Sys.getenv("OPAL_ADMIN_PW"),
                url = "https://nairobi.datashield.live", opts = opts)
m <- dsadmin.get_methods(o, type = "aggregate")
m[grepl("flowerFeatureStatsDS", m$name), c("name", "type", "class")]
#>                    name      type    class
#> 24 flowerFeatureStatsDS aggregate function   ->  dsFlower::flowerFeatureStatsDS

The client can now call it. (Everything else in dsFlower — the run lifecycle, the DP budget query, the training methods — was registered by the same dsadmin.set_package_methods() call.)

4. Using it against the live federation

Log in to the three sites and assign the demo table to the symbol D:

library(DSI); library(DSOpal); library(dsFlowerClient)

builder <- newDSLoginBuilder()
for (h in hosts) {
  builder$append(
    server = h, url = paste0("https://", h, ".datashield.live"),
    user = "administrator", password = Sys.getenv("OPAL_ADMIN_PW"),
    table = "dsflower_demo.breast_cancer", driver = "OpalDriver",
    options = "list(ssl_verifyhost=0L, ssl_verifypeer=0L)")
}
conns <- datashield.login(builder$build(), assign = TRUE, symbol = "D")

datashield.aggregate(conns, quote(dimDS("D")))
#> $nairobi
#> [1] 190  31
#> $dakar
#> [1] 190  31
#> $douala
#> [1] 189  31

569 patients across three countries — and not one row leaves a site. We can call our newly registered method directly to see the disclosure-controlled statistics it returns, and pool them into a global mean exactly as the training pipeline does:

st <- datashield.aggregate(conns, call("flowerFeatureStatsDS", "D", "mean_radius"))
tot_n <- sum(vapply(st, `[[`, 0, "n"))
tot_s <- sum(vapply(st, `[[`, 0, "sum"))
tot_s / tot_n                       # global mean of mean_radius, pooled over all sites
#> nairobi mean_radius: n = 190, sum = 2683.6, sumsq = 39880
#> GLOBAL mean_radius (pooled over 569 patients): 14.127

In practice you never call it by hand — ds.flower.fit() does it for you, uses the pooled mean/SD to standardize the features, and bakes the same statistics into the model so prediction scales new data identically. Train a federated, DP-protected model in one call:

run_lr  <- ds.flower.fit(conns, target = "malignant", model = "logreg",  rounds = 5L)
run_xgb <- ds.flower.fit(conns, target = "malignant", model = "xgboost", rounds = 5L)

5. Results

Predicting on a held-out copy of the data (test), against the majority-class baseline of 0.63:

mean(as.integer(ds.flower.predict(run_lr,  test)) == test$malignant)
mean(as.integer(ds.flower.predict(run_xgb, test)) == test$malignant)
Model Mechanism Accuracy (ε = 3) Majority baseline
logreg DP-SGD (Opacus) 0.931 0.63
xgboost DP-GBDT (S-GBDT) 0.926 0.63

Both are trained with differential privacy on (ε = 3) and never see a single raw row on the client. The DP cost is small once the pipeline is correct — which is precisely what flowerFeatureStatsDS makes possible (global standardization at no extra privacy budget).

The trees run reports an honest federation summary:

#> xgboost history: n_boosters = 3, n_failures = 0

Finally, a quick node health check — flowerGetCapabilitiesDS() also exposes a defunct-process counter for monitoring:

caps <- datashield.aggregate(conns, quote(flowerGetCapabilitiesDS()))
#> nairobi: dsFlower 0.2.4, zombie_processes = 0
#> dakar:   dsFlower 0.2.4, zombie_processes = 0
#> douala:  dsFlower 0.2.4, zombie_processes = 0
datashield.logout(conns)

Recap

  1. A server-side method is R code declared in a package’s DESCRIPTION/NAMESPACE and registered with Opal (dsadmin.set_package_methods()), after which whitelisted clients may call it.
  2. flowerFeatureStatsDS is our example — a disclosure-controlled aggregate that lets dsFlower standardize features globally so DP-protected models stay accurate.
  3. Against the live *.datashield.live federation, a one-line ds.flower.fit() trains a federated model with server-enforced differential privacy and reaches ~0.93 accuracy on the Breast-Cancer-Wisconsin demo — with the raw data never leaving the sites.
